name: Posture / frame / body language

image.caption: Yerevan, Armenian girls posing in photo shoot, Acting, Posture, Body language, Armenia

lead: Posture, frame and body language practices use an upright, open and expansive stance so you look taller, broader and more confident while standing and moving. The visual change is immediate.

The chain: open posture gives a taller, broader impression, which makes you look and feel more confident. Studies show small effects on how powerful people feel; the hormonal and behavioural effects reported for power posing in 2010 have not replicated well, and reviews find a reliable effect on feelings of power but not physiology.

paras: People practise standing tall with shoulders back, an open chest and head level, and use power poses before events. It is combined with back and core training and is a free habit that can show in photos right away.
No direct risks reported. There is ongoing disagreement about effect sizes for the feeling-of-power research.

angle.text: Users hold an upright, open stance, sometimes as power posing, so they look taller, broader and more confident while standing. The visual change is immediate; hormone and behaviour claims from posing have replicated poorly, while effects on how people feel are better supported.

lead: In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities, "posture", "frame" and "body language" describe how a person holds and moves their body. Practitioners use upright, open and expansive postures to look taller, broader-shouldered, more athletic and more self-assured, because the way the head, shoulders and spine are stacked changes the silhouette others see and the impression of confidence a person gives off.

Posture work in these communities usually targets visible alignment: pulling the head back from a forward position, setting the shoulders back and down, and standing or sitting tall. Posture and body language are also discussed as an attractiveness signal, alongside "power posing", the popular idea that holding expansive poses boosts feelings of power.[1][2]

Research on posture reports that confident postures can influence self-evaluation and mood. Reviews find a reliable effect of power poses on feelings of power, while the hormonal and behavioral claims of the original 2010 study have not replicated well.[1][2] Separate physiotherapy literature has studied corrective exercise for forward head posture and rounded shoulders, and reports measurable changes in craniovertebral angle.[3][4]
infobox: Power posing, posture correction, tongue posture
Forward head posture, rounded shoulders, slouching

paras: "Posture" refers to the position of the head, spine, shoulders and pelvis at rest and in motion. "Frame" is community shorthand for the overall impression of a body: shoulder width, carriage, stillness and presence. "Body language" covers gestures, stance and movement that others read as confidence, interest or indifference.

Looksmaxxing forum users describe posture as a "multiplier" for the face and body, arguing that identical features look different depending on head position and spinal alignment.[5][6] One widely read thread frames the skull as a lever whose orientation depends on posture, and attributes forward head position to overactive upper traps and weak lower trap and back muscles.[5]

Practitioners point to several visual effects: standing tall adds apparent height, drawing the shoulders back widens the upper body, and bringing the head back over the shoulders changes the look of the neck and jawline. Some forum members also report that correcting forward head posture changes how the face projects in profile, and some debate whether it makes a recessed face look more or less recessed.[7]

Physiotherapy research defines forward head posture, rounded shoulders and thoracic hyperkyphosis as common postural patterns and measures them with angles such as the craniovertebral angle.[8][3] These measures are the closest clinical counterpart to what looksmaxxing communities call posture fixing.

Carney, Cuddy and Yap (2010) reported that holding expansive poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol in 42 participants. Ranehill et al. (2015) replicated only the felt-power effect, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real.[1] A 2022 review of 128 studies by Korner et al. found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, none on physiology and unclear effects on behavior; Cuddy and colleagues' 2018 meta-analysis reported evidential value for postural feedback.[1]

Brinol, Petty and Wagner (2009) found that people writing self-descriptions in a confident posture rated themselves more favorably than those in a doubtful posture, and Riskind and Gotay (1982) reported more stress in hunched postures.[2] Open posture was rated as more capable in counseling settings (Ridley and Asbury, 1988).[2] Peper et al. (2018) reported better math scores with erect posture.[2]

A meta-analysis of seven randomized trials with 627 participants found that corrective exercise changed the craniovertebral angle in people with forward head posture and reduced pain.[4] A 2024 meta-analysis of exercise for upper crossed syndrome examined forward head posture, rounded shoulders and hyperkyphosis together.[3] A review of the link between forward head posture and neck pain reported a significant difference in adults with neck pain but not in adolescents.[8]

Forum members discuss posture across several threads, from basic how-to questions to long guides, and often link it with tongue posture (mewing), neck training and back work.[9][10] Some users describe posture as overlooked relative to surgery or skincare; others are skeptical of social-media posture routines.[10]

Studies of posture and mood exist, and power-posing trials are summarized above.[1][2] Exercise trials have measured changes in forward head posture, rounded shoulders and kyphosis.[3][4] No studies were found testing "frame" as defined by looksmaxxing communities.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org posture is discussed as a foundational, low-cost way to improve appearance and is frequently tied to jaw and neck position.[9][5]
